newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Deadlock in plans to help Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: Deadlock in plans to help Zaire refugees.

text.p: Efforts to help 1.2 million refugees stranded in the war zone of eastern Zaire reached stalemate on Wednesday, with Zaire telling aid agencies to keep out and the U.N. saying many lives were at risk.

"We are asking humanitarian organisations to stop distributing any aid to the refugees on Zairean soil. They must instead distribute aid in Rwanda and Burundi," said Zairean spokesman Boguo Makeli, whose government wants the refugees out.
Aid dried up last week when aid workers fled fighting. The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR says many lives will be lost unless they take food and medicine back into Zaire fast.
"You can't repatriate dead refugees. We need to get in there," its spokesman Peter Kessler told Reuters in Nairobi.
An eight-nation African summit in Nairobi on Tuesday called for the U.N. to send a "neutral" protection force to create havens from which they could go home along safe corridors.

France, pushing the hardest for intervention, wants the force to be 5,000-strong and multinational, its ally Spain said. Both have pledged around 1,000 troops, but Rwanda considers Paris pro-Hutu and is believed to want France to stay away.
The United States, Africans and others France and Spain want to entice in seemed lukewarm.

African nations only plan their next formal discussion of the force next Monday, Britain said it was far too early to consider and analysts said post-election Washington had other things to occupy it.
"U.S. interest in most of sub-Saharan Africa is minimal," said Michael Cox, an analyst of U.S. foreign policy.

All the time, the plight of the refugees, most of whom fled from Rwanda after militant Hutus killed up to a million mainly Tutsis in the genocide of 1994, gets worse. Kessler said some had had no food for nearly three weeks.
Even a ceasefire by the rebels in Zaire, whose leader Laurent Kabila was a comrade-in-arms of 1960s Marxist guerrilla Che Guevara, has not eased access to refugees behind Zairean lines.

In the rebel-held eastern Zairean of Goma, Zairean aid workers were unable to reach the world's largest refugee camp Mugunga because rebels said it was held by Interahamwe Hutu militiamen, who had a major role in Rwanda's 1994 genocide.

Analysts said the Zairean rebels, who have scored stunning advances in east Zaire, are split over whether to fight on against Zaire's army or seek a political settlement with the leaders of one of Africa's least stable states.

In the east, the rebels are mainly native Tutsis who rose up two weeks ago when Zaire decided to expel them. They are allied to various groups opposed to President Mobutu Sese Seko, whose grip on power spans three decades rife with corruption.
Mobutu, convalescing in France after surgery that has kept him away for months, was to meet special U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien to discuss the crisis on Wednesday.

Zaire and the rest of the world want the refugees to go home. But they fear retribution for the genocide which was carried out by Hutu militiamen who have used the refugee camps as their shields for over two years.
The Hutu soldiers in Zaire are well armed. A U.N. report obtained on Tuesday showed they had been amply supplied with arms from Europe and South Africa.
South Africa said on Wednesday it had suspended supplying arms to the Rwandan Tutsi-led government, having consulted regional leaders after reports of Rwandan incursions into Zaire.
Aid is piled high in Rwanda, awaiting the refugees' return, and aid agencies are flying planeloads of additional medical supplies into Kenya and Uganda, waiting to help.

So far only 2,000 have ventured home to Rwanda, while 11,000 Burundian Hutu refugees have been forced home by Zairean rebels. Burundian returnees report some were taken away on arrival and, they fear, executed.
Aid agencies are exasperated, fearing that every day brings nearer a repeat of the 1994 catastrophe in which 50,000 Rwandan refugees died from disease in just two months.
"We should intervene immediately," European Union special envoy Aldo Ajello told a Nairobi news conference. "Or at least as soon as possible. The framework should be very short."
